items.title: Selling into the bids
items.prose: This is the order book for one share. You hold 1,200 shares and send a market order to sell them all at once.
items.question: Tap every price level your order trades at.

feedback.correct: 600 shares fill at £250.40 and the other 600 at £250.38.
feedback.generic: A sell trades with buyers. Take the best bid first, then the next, until 1,200 shares are done.

byKey.asks: You tapped the asks. Those are other sellers; a market sell trades with the bids.
byKey.ask0: You tapped an ask. A market sell trades with buyers, on the bid side.
byKey.bid0: The best bid, £250.40, fills first. Price priority sends a sell there before any lower bid.
byKey.bid1: Only 600 shares wait at £250.40. The other 600 go to the next bid, £250.38.
byKey.bid2: The order is done at £250.38: 600 of the 900 there finish the 1,200.

explain.text: A market sell walks down the bids. It takes 600 at £250.40, then 600 of the 900 at £250.38. Its average price is £250.39, a penny below the best bid.

items.title: A forward from spot and carry
items.prose: A share trades at £40.00 and pays no dividend in the next year. You can borrow and lend at 4% a year, compounded yearly. Analysts expect the share to be £45.00 in a year.
items.question: What is the no-arbitrage one-year forward price?

options.why: You used the analysts' forecast. The forward is what buying now and financing costs, not a prediction.
You left out the carry. Holding the share for a year costs a year's interest on £40.00.
You discounted the spot price. Carrying the share forward grows it: multiply by 1.04.

feedback.correct: Borrow £40.00, buy the share, and repay £41.60 in a year.
feedback.generic: Price the forward as the cost of buying today with borrowed money.

explain.text: Borrowing £40.00 at 4% and buying the share delivers it in a year for $40 \times 1.04 = 41.60$ pounds. Any other forward price lets someone lock in a riskless profit. The £45.00 forecast plays no part.

items.title: Placing a put's strike
items.prose: You buy a put for £4.00. The diagram shows its profit at expiry. Drag the diamond on the price axis to move the strike.
items.question: Drag the strike so that the put breaks even when the share ends at £91.00.

feedback.correct: A strike of £95.00 puts the break-even at $95 - 4 = 91$.
feedback.generic: A long put breaks even at $K - p$. Solve $K - 4 = 91$.

byKey.subtracted: You set the strike at £87.00, the break-even less the premium. A put breaks even below its strike, so add the premium.
byKey.no-premium: At a strike of £91.00 the put pays nothing at £91.00, so you are still down the £4.00 premium.
byKey.p1: Not yet. A long put's break-even is its strike less the premium.

explain.text: At £91.00 a £95.00 put pays £4.00, exactly what it cost. Below £91.00 the profit is positive. Above the strike it is −£4.00, the premium.

items.title: The risk-neutral weight
items.prose: A one-step tree. A share at £80.00 moves in a year to £100.00 or £72.00. Cash grows by $1 + r$ over the step, with $r = 4\%$.

state.caption: One year; cash grows by $1 + r$ with $r = 4\%$

items.question: What is the risk-neutral probability $q$ of the up move?

feedback.correct: Under $q = 0.4$ the share is expected to reach £83.20, which is $80 \times 1.04$.
feedback.generic: Write $u$ and $d$ as factors, then use $q = \dfrac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}$.

byKey.no-interest: You grew cash by 1, not 1.04. Under $q$ the share must grow like cash.
byKey.down: You found the weight on the down move, $1 - q$.

items.title: Skewing for inventory
items.prose: You make a market around a fair value $V = 1{,}250$p, with half-spread $s = 1.5$p. Your rule centres quotes on $m = V - \gamma q$, with $\gamma = 0.5$p per lot. Sellers have hit your bid four times, so you hold $q = +4$ lots.
items.question: Fill in your new quotes, in pence.

feedback.correct: Both quotes fall 2p, so a sale becomes likelier than another purchase.
feedback.generic: Centre on $V - \gamma q$, then quote $m - s$ and $m + s$.

byKey.r0c1: Long inventory moves the centre down: $1{,}250 - 0.5 \times 4 = 1{,}248$p.
byKey.r1c1: The bid sits 1.5p below the centre.
byKey.r2c1: The ask sits 1.5p above the centre.

explain.text: Long 4 lots, you want to sell, so both quotes fall by $0.5 \times 4 = 2$p. The bid at 1,246.5p discourages more sellers, and the ask at 1,249.5p draws buyers. The spread stays 3p.

items.title: Comparing savings rates
items.prose:
Three one-year savings accounts quote nominal annual rates.
- A: 5.40%, credited daily, each day earning 5.40%/365.
- B: 5.50%, credited once, at the end of the year.
- C: 5.45%, credited quarterly.
items.question: Which account leaves you with the most after a year?

options.why: You assumed the most frequent credit wins. Daily 5.40% is 5.548% effective, below C's 5.562%.
You compared nominal rates. B is credited once, so its effective rate is just 5.50%.
You treated the quotes as equivalent. Only effective rates compare, and they differ.

feedback.correct: C's quarterly credits make 5.562% effective, the most of the three.
feedback.generic: Turn each quote into an effective rate, $(1 + r/m)^m - 1$, then compare.

explain.text: A grows by $(1 + 0.054/365)^{365} = 1.05548$. B grows by 1.05500 and C by $(1 + 0.0545/4)^4 = 1.05562$. So C is best, though it quotes less than B.

items.title: A put from its call
items.prose: A six-month European call struck at £50.00 costs £6.50. The share is at £48.00 and pays no dividend. The rate is 4% a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: What must the European put with the same strike and expiry cost? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: Parity gives $p = c + K/(1+r)^T - S_0 = 7.53$ pounds.
feedback.generic: Use $c + \dfrac{K}{(1+r)^T} = p + S_0$ with $T = 0.5$.

byKey.undisc: You subtracted the £50.00 strike as if paid today. It is paid in six months, so discount it.
byKey.full-year: You discounted the strike for a whole year. Six months is $T = 0.5$.
byKey.flipped: You swapped the sides of parity. The put sits with the share: $p + S_0 = c + K/(1+r)^T$.

explain.text: $50/1.04^{0.5} = 49.03$, so the call side is $6.50 + 49.03 = 55.53$. The put side is $p + 48$, so $p = 7.53$. The put is dearer than the call because the share sits below the strike.

items.title: Fills against the arrival price
items.prose: You must buy 3,000 shares now, and the book is as shown. The **arrival price** is the mid when you send the order: £25.00. The volume-weighted average price of your fills is your VWAP.
items.question: You send a market buy for 3,000 shares. What is its VWAP's slippage against the arrival price, in basis points? Give one decimal place.

feedback.correct: The VWAP is £25.034, 3.4p over the arrival mid: 13.6 bp.
feedback.generic: Walk the asks for 3,000 shares, find the average fill price, then compare it with £25.00 in bp.

byKey.vs-ask: You measured from the best ask. The arrival price is the mid, half a spread lower.
byKey.plain-average: You averaged the three prices equally. Weight each by the shares filled there: only 1,000 fill at £25.05.
byKey.pence: That is the slippage in pence a share. Divide by the £25.00 arrival price and multiply by 10,000.

explain.text: The fills are 800 at £25.02, 1,200 at £25.03 and 1,000 at £25.05, costing £75,102. The VWAP is $75{,}102/3{,}000 = 25.034$ pounds. Slippage is $0.034/25 \times 10{,}000 = 13.6$ bp: 8 bp of half-spread and 5.6 bp of walking the book.

items.title: A European put over two steps
items.prose: A share at £100.00 is multiplied by $u = 1.1$ or $d = 0.9$ at each of two steps. Cash grows by $1 + r$ per step, with $r = 2\%$ per step. A European put struck at £100.00 expires at the end of step 2.

state.caption: Cash grows by $1 + r$ per step, $r = 2\%$

items.question: What is the put worth today? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: Backward induction gives £0.39 at £110.00, £8.04 at £90.00, then £3.38 today.
feedback.generic: Find $q = \dfrac{1.02 - 0.9}{1.1 - 0.9}$, price the leaves, then step back twice.

byKey.one-disc: You discounted once. The payoff is two steps away, so divide by $1.02^2$.
byKey.no-two: You weighted the middle leaf once. Two paths reach £99.00: up then down, and down then up.
byKey.flipped: You put $q$ on the down move. Here $q = 0.6$ is the weight on up.

items.title: Pricing a bond
items.prose: A bond has a face value of £100.00 and four years to maturity. It pays a 3% coupon once a year, the next in exactly a year. Its yield is 4.5% a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: What is the bond's price? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: The yield is above the coupon rate, so the bond trades at a discount: £94.62.
feedback.generic: Discount each £3.00 coupon and the £100.00 face at 4.5% for its own wait.

byKey.at-coupon: You discounted at the coupon rate. Discount at the 4.5% yield; the coupon only sets the cash flows.
byKey.face-undisc: You added the £100.00 face without discounting it. It is paid in four years.
byKey.coupons-undisc: You added the four £3.00 coupons without discounting them.
byKey.no-face: You left out the £100.00 repaid at maturity.

explain.text: The coupons are worth $3 \times \dfrac{1 - 1.045^{-4}}{0.045} = 10.76$ pounds. The face is worth $100/1.045^4 = 83.86$ pounds. Together they make £94.62.

items.title: A bear put spread
items.prose: On one share you buy a put struck at £60.00 for £5.20. You also sell a put struck at £52.00 for £1.70. Both expire on the same day. The bold line is the spread's profit at expiry.
items.question: Fill in the spread's key numbers, in pounds.

rows: Profit if the share ends at £55.00

feedback.correct: Net cost £3.50, capped profit £4.50 and break-even £56.50.
feedback.generic: Net the two premiums. The payoff is capped at the £8.00 gap between the strikes.

byKey.r0c1: Net the premiums: you pay £5.20 and receive £1.70.
byKey.r1c1: The payoff is capped at $60 - 52 = 8$ pounds. Take off the net cost.
byKey.r2c1: Break-even is the upper strike less the net cost.
byKey.r3c1: At £55.00 only the 60 put pays: £5.00, less the £3.50 cost.

explain.text: You pay $5.20 - 1.70 = 3.50$ pounds. Below £52.00 the payoff is the full £8.00, so the most you make is £4.50. You break even at $60 - 3.50 = 56.50$, and at £55.00 you make $5 - 3.50 = 1.50$.

items.title: When a limit order pays
items.prose: A share is quoted £12.47 bid and £12.53 ask, a mid of £12.50. You want to buy. A market order pays 3p over the mid. A limit buy at the bid fills with chance $p$, saving 3p against the mid. If it misses, you chase and pay 7p over the mid.
items.question: At what fill chance $p$ do the two orders have the same expected cost?

feedback.correct: At $p = 0.4$ both cost 3p a share; above it the limit is cheaper.
feedback.generic: Write the limit's expected cost as $-3p + 7(1 - p)$ pence and set it equal to 3.

byKey.no-save: You gave a fill no value. A limit filled at the bid saves the half-spread: its cost is −3p.
byKey.half: You split the difference. Solve $-3p + 7(1 - p) = 3$ for $p$.

explain.text: The limit costs $-3p + 7(1 - p) = 7 - 10p$ pence on average. Setting $7 - 10p = 3$ gives $p = 0.4$. It matches the rule $p > c/(2h + c) = 4/10$, with $h = 3$p and $c = 4$p.

items.title: Hedging a book of short calls
items.prose: A one-step tree: a share at £50.00 moves in a year to £60.00 or £42.00. Cash grows by $1 + r$ over the step, with $r = 3\%$. A dealer has sold 9,000 calls struck at £50.00, each on one share. She hedges with shares bought on borrowed cash.

state.caption: One year; cash grows by $1 + r$ with $r = 3\%$

items.question: Fill in the hedge and the call's price. Type numbers without commas.

rows: Shares to buy for the 9,000 calls

feedback.correct: 5,000 shares, £203,883.50 borrowed, and £5.12 a call.
feedback.generic: Find $\Delta = \dfrac{c_u - c_d}{S_u - S_d}$, then the loan that the down state repays.

byKey.r0c1: Delta is $\dfrac{10 - 0}{60 - 42} = \dfrac{5}{9}$ per call. Multiply by 9,000.
byKey.r1c1: In the down state the shares are worth £42.00 each and the calls nothing. Borrow that amount discounted by 1.03.
byKey.r2c1: One call costs its copy: shares bought less cash borrowed, per call.

explain.text: $\Delta = 10/18 = 5/9$, so 9,000 short calls need 5,000 shares. In the down state they are worth £210,000 and the calls nothing, so borrow $210{,}000/1.03 = 203{,}883.50$. The shares cost £250,000, so one call costs $(250{,}000 - 203{,}883.50)/9{,}000 = 5.12$ pounds.

items.title: A fund's annualised return
items.prose: A fund's factsheet shows four yearly total returns: +25%, −20%, +10% and +6%. Gains are reinvested.
items.question: What is its annualised return? Give a percentage to two decimal places.

feedback.correct: £1 grows to £1.166, which is 3.91% a year compounded.
feedback.generic: Multiply the four growth factors, take the fourth root, then subtract 1.

byKey.arith: You averaged the four returns. Returns compound, so a 20% fall costs more than a 25% gain makes back.
byKey.simple: You divided the total return by 4. Annualise with a fourth root instead.
byKey.total: That is the total over four years. The question asks for the steady yearly rate.

explain.text: The growth factors multiply: $1.25 \times 0.8 \times 1.1 \times 1.06 = 1.166$. The annualised return is $1.166^{1/4} - 1 = 0.0391$, or 3.91% a year. The arithmetic mean, 5.25%, overstates it.

items.title: Delta of a short call book
items.prose: A trader is short 800 calls and long 500 puts on one share, each option on one share. Each call has delta 0.45 and each put delta −0.30.
items.question: How many shares must she buy to make the book delta neutral? Use a negative number to sell.

feedback.correct: The book's delta is −510 shares, so buy 510.
feedback.generic: Add quantity times delta for each line, with short positions negative. Then trade the opposite.

byKey.put-sign: You gave the long puts a positive delta. A put's delta is negative, so they add to the short calls' exposure.
byKey.calls-only: You hedged the calls and ignored the puts. 500 long puts at −0.30 add −150.
byKey.sell: You flipped the sign. The book's delta is −510, so buying 510 shares brings it to zero.

explain.text: The short calls give $-800 \times 0.45 = -360$ and the long puts $500 \times (-0.30) = -150$. The book loses like 510 shares short when the share rises. Buying 510 shares makes it delta neutral.

items.title: A call's price as a function of its strike
items.prose: A one-step tree: a share at £100.00 moves in a year to £120.00 or £80.00. Cash grows by $1 + r$ over the step, with $r = 5\%$, so $q = 0.625$. A European call is struck at $K$, with $80 \le K \le 120$.
items.question: Write the call's price today in terms of $K$.

feedback.correct: The call pays $120 - K$ only in the up state, so $c = 0.625(120 - K)/1.05$.
feedback.generic: In the down state the call pays 0. Weight the up payoff by $q$ and discount once.

byKey.no-disc: You took the $q$-weighted payoff but did not discount it by 1.05.
byKey.half: You weighted up and down equally. The weight on up is $q = 0.625$, not 0.5.

explain.text: At £80.00 the call pays nothing, and at £120.00 it pays $120 - K$. So $c = \dfrac{0.625(120 - K)}{1.05} = \dfrac{25(120 - K)}{42}$. At $K = 100$ that is £11.90, the price from the course.

items.title: Quoting against informed traders
items.prose: Before results, a share is worth 512p or 488p, equally likely, so $V = 500$p. A quarter of traders know which: they buy if it is 512p and sell if it is 488p. The rest buy or sell at random, each with chance $\tfrac12$.
items.question: What ask, in pence, breaks even on average against the next buy order?

feedback.correct: Given a buy, the value is 512p with chance 0.625, so $E[V \mid \text{buy}] = 503$p.
feedback.generic: Find $P(512 \mid \text{buy})$ with Bayes' rule, then the expected value given a buy.

byKey.fair: You quoted at the value before the trade. A buy is evidence for 512p, so the value given a buy is higher.
byKey.all-informed: You treated every buyer as informed. Three quarters trade at random.
byKey.double: You gave a buy a 0.75 chance of meaning 512p. Random buyers come in both states, so it is 0.625.

explain.text: At 512p a trader buys with chance $0.25 + 0.75 \times 0.5 = 0.625$, and at 488p with chance 0.375. So $P(512 \mid \text{buy}) = 0.625$ and $E[V \mid \text{buy}] = 0.625 \times 512 + 0.375 \times 488 = 503$p. The half-spread of $\alpha\delta = 0.25 \times 12 = 3$p pays for losses to the informed.

items.title: A short sale that goes wrong
items.prose: You short 2,000 shares at £24.00 and cover two months later at £26.50. The stock loan fee is 4% a year on the £48,000.00 sale value, charged for 2/12 of a year. While you are short, the company pays a dividend of £0.30 a share.
items.question: What is your profit, in pounds? Use a negative number for a loss.

feedback.correct: −£5,000.00 on the share, −£320.00 of fee and −£600.00 of dividend: −£5,920.00.
feedback.generic: Profit is $P_0 - P_1$ a share, less the fee and the dividends you pay the lender.

byKey.no-cost: You left out the fee and the dividend. A short pays both.
byKey.div-received: You received the dividend. The lender is owed it, so the short pays £600.00.
byKey.full-year: You charged a full year's fee. Two months is 2/12 of 4% on £48,000.00, which is £320.00.

explain.text: On the shares you lose $2{,}000 \times (26.50 - 24.00) = 5{,}000$ pounds. The fee is $48{,}000 \times 0.04 \times 2/12 = 320$ pounds and the dividend $2{,}000 \times 0.30 = 600$ pounds. In all you lose £5,920.00.

items.title: Parity through a forward
items.prose: We derive put-call parity for European options on a share with no dividend. Both options have strike $K$ and expiry $T$ years. The rate is $r$ a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Hold a long call and a short put, both struck at $K$.
Above $K$ the call pays $S_T - K$. Below $K$ the short put pays $-(K - S_T)$. Either way they pay $S_T - K$.
One share bought today with $K/(1+r)^T$ borrowed also pays $S_T - K$ at expiry.
That share and loan cost $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$ today; the options cost $c - p$.
Equal payoffs must cost the same, or buying the cheap side and selling the dear one is riskless profit.
So $c - p = S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$, which rearranges to $c + K/(1+r)^T = p + S_0$.

feedback.correct: Call minus put is a forward at $K$, and the forward is a share less a loan.
feedback.generic: Start from the options' payoff, find a second portfolio with the same payoff, then price both.

explain.text: A long call and a short put pay $S_T - K$, like a long forward at price $K$. A share bought with $K/(1+r)^T$ borrowed pays the same and costs $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$. Equal payoffs force equal prices, and that is parity.

items.title: A quick price for an at-the-money call
items.prose: A share is at £250.00. A three-month European call is struck at £250.00. Take $\sigma = 30\%$ and $r = 0$.

parts.question: Use the rule $0.4\,\sigma\sqrt T\,S$. What price does it give?

feedback.generic: Multiply $0.4$, $\sigma$, $\sqrt T$ and $S$. Three months is $T = 0.25$.

byKey.no-root: You left out the square root of time: $0.4\sigma S$ is for one year.
byKey.time-not-root: You used $T$, not $\sqrt T$. A quarter of a year gives $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$, not 0.25.

parts.question: Implied volatility rises from 30% to 32%. About how much does the call gain? Use vega $\approx$ price $\div\,\sigma$.

feedback.generic: Vega is price over $\sigma$, per 1.00 of vol. Scale it by the rise in $\sigma$.

byKey.points-as-units: You took vega per 1.00 of vol, 50, and multiplied by 2. Two points is 0.02 of vol.
byKey.one-point: That is one vol point, 0.50. The rise is two points.

parts.question: Now one month is left, with the same strike and vol. What does the rule give?

feedback.generic: The rule goes like $\sqrt T$. One month is a third of three.

byKey.by-time: You scaled the price by the time left, a third. It scales by the square root, $1/\sqrt 3$.
byKey.unchanged: At the money the price still falls as time runs down: it goes like $\sqrt T$.

explain.text: $0.4 \times 0.3 \times \sqrt{0.25} \times 250 = 15.00$. Price is linear in $\sigma$ and goes like $\sqrt T$. So two vol points add $15/0.3 \times 0.02 = 1.00$, and a month left gives $15/\sqrt 3 = 8.66$.

Those are the long put's signs. Selling the put flips every one.

You read gamma as following delta's level. Gamma is delta's slope, and delta is flat out there.

options.why: Gamma changes with the share price. It peaks near the strike, at £94.18 here.

parts.prose: She sold 1,000 of the puts, each on one share. Each has gamma 0.0198 per £1 at a share price of £100. She priced them at 20% volatility and hedges delta every day. Over the next 21 trading days (252 in a year) the share's realised volatility is 28%. Treat gamma as constant.
parts.question: What is her hedged P&L in pounds? Use a negative number for a loss.

feedback.correct: About −£317: she is short gamma and realised volatility beat implied.
feedback.generic: Use $\tfrac12\Gamma S^2 \times$ (realised variance minus implied variance) $\times$ time, with the sign of a short position.

byKey.sign: You gave her the long option's P&L. She is short gamma, so realised above implied costs her.
byKey.no-half: You left out the half in $\tfrac12\Gamma S^2$.
byKey.vol-gap: You used the gap in volatilities, 0.08. The formula uses the gap in variances, $0.28^2 - 0.20^2 = 0.0384$.
byKey.no-time: You counted a whole year of variance. Only 21 of 252 days passed.

items.title: A market maker that skews
items.prose: Simulate a market maker's day. A client `"buy"` takes your ask and a `"sell"` hits your bid, one lot each. Before each client, centre your quotes on $m = V - \gamma q$. When `q == limit` you show no bid, and when `q == -limit` no ask. That client trades elsewhere.
items.question: Complete `make_market(flow, V, s, gamma, limit)` so it returns `[q, cash, pnl]`.

widget.starter:
def make_market(flow, V, s, gamma, limit):
    """flow: client orders, each "buy" or "sell".
    Centre m = V - gamma * q, q in lots.
    Bid m - s, ask m + s, in pence. A lot is
    100 shares: a lot at x pence is x pounds.
    Return [q, cash, pnl], pnl marked at V."""
    q = 0
    cash = 0.0
    for side in flow:
        m = ...
        if side == "buy":   # client takes your ask
            ...
        else:               # client hits your bid
            ...
    pnl = cash + q * V
    return [q, round(cash, 6), round(pnl, 6)]
widget.solution:
def make_market(flow, V, s, gamma, limit):
    """flow: client orders, each "buy" or "sell".
    Centre m = V - gamma * q, q in lots.
    Bid m - s, ask m + s, in pence. A lot is
    100 shares: a lot at x pence is x pounds.
    Return [q, cash, pnl], pnl marked at V."""
    q = 0
    cash = 0.0
    for side in flow:
        m = V - gamma * q
        if side == "buy":   # client takes your ask
            if q == -limit:   # no ask at the limit
                continue
            cash += m + s
            q -= 1
        else:               # client hits your bid
            if q == limit:    # no bid at the limit
                continue
            cash -= m - s
            q += 1
    pnl = cash + q * V
    return [q, round(cash, 6), round(pnl, 6)]
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Each returned list is compared item by item with `math.isclose`; cash and P&L are rounded to 6 places. The first run starts Python in your browser, which can take 10 to 20 seconds. Later runs are quick.

byKey.r0c1: Use $d_1 = \dfrac{\ln(80/75) + (0.03 + 0.25^2/2) \times 0.5}{0.25\sqrt{0.5}}$. The denominator is $\sigma\sqrt T$, not $\sigma$.

parts.question: A client asks for a digital call instead: £1 paid in six months if the share is above £75.00. What is its price, to four decimal places?

feedback.generic: A digital call is $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$. Use $d_2$ from the table above.

byKey.no-discount: You gave the risk-neutral chance, $\Phi(d_2)$. The £1 arrives in six months, so discount it by $e^{-0.015}$.
byKey.d1-slip: You used $\Phi(d_1)$, the call's delta. A digital uses $\Phi(d_2)$.

explain.text: A digital call is $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) = e^{-0.015} \times 0.6412 = 0.6316$. It is the limit of a tight call spread divided by its width.

widget.solution:
import math

def put_prices(S, K, r, sigma, T, n):
    """European and American puts, n-step CRR.
    Cash grows by exp(r * dt) per step.
    Return [european, american], 6 places."""
    dt = T / n
    u = math.exp(sigma * math.sqrt(dt))
    d = 1 / u
    q = (math.exp(r * dt) - d) / (u - d)
    disc = math.exp(-r * dt)
    # leaves: j is the number of up moves
    euro = [max(K - S * u ** j * d ** (n - j), 0) for j in range(n + 1)]
    amer = euro[:]
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        # back to time i: nodes j = 0..i
        euro = [disc * (q * euro[j + 1] + (1 - q) * euro[j]) for j in range(i + 1)]
        amer = [max(disc * (q * amer[j + 1] + (1 - q) * amer[j]),
                    K - S * u ** j * d ** (i - j)) for j in range(i + 1)]
    return [round(euro[0], 6), round(amer[0], 6)]

explain.text: Each step back replaces neighbours with their discounted $q$-average. The American list then takes a max with $K - Su^jd^{i-j}$, the exercise value at that node. The gap is the early-exercise premium, and it vanishes when $r = 0$.

items.title: Quoting a client's call
items.prompt:
A client asks you to quote 5,000 three-month European calls struck at £48.00, each on one share. The share is at £50.00 and pays no dividend. Use $r = 4\%$ a year, compounded continuously, and $\sigma = 30\%$.

(a) Bound the call's price without a model.

(b) Price one call on a two-step CRR tree: $\Delta t = 0.125$, $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$, $d = 1/u$, and cash growing by $e^{r\Delta t}$ per step.

(c) You sell the 5,000 calls. Give the hedge today, and say how it changes after one step.

(d) What do you quote, and which risks remain after the hedge?
items.model:
**(a)** A call is worth at most the share, $c \le 50$. A call plus cash $Ke^{-rT}$ pays at least one share at expiry, so $c \ge S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$. Here $Ke^{-rT} = 48e^{-0.01} = 47.52$, so $2.48 \le c \le 50$. The floor beats the £2.00 intrinsic value because the strike is paid later.

**(b)** $u = e^{0.3\sqrt{0.125}} = 1.11190$ and $d = 0.89937$. A step grows cash by $e^{0.005} = 1.005013$, so $q = (1.005013 - 0.89937)/(1.11190 - 0.89937) = 0.4971$. The share reaches £55.59 or £44.97 after one step, and £61.82, £50.00 or £40.44 at expiry. The call pays £13.82, £2.00 and £0 there.

At the up node: $(0.4971 \times 13.82 + 0.5029 \times 2)/1.005013 = 7.83$. At the down node: $(0.4971 \times 2)/1.005013 = 0.99$. Today: $(0.4971 \times 7.83 + 0.5029 \times 0.99)/1.005013 = 4.37$. That sits inside the bounds. Black-Scholes, the many-step limit, gives about £4.32, so two steps are close but coarse.

**(c)** $\Delta_0 = (7.83 - 0.99)/(55.59 - 44.97) = 0.6441$. Short 5,000 calls, so buy about 3,221 shares for £161,035. The £21,849 premium pays part, and you borrow about £139,185. After an up step both leaves are in the money and delta is 1: buy up to 5,000 shares. After a down step delta is $2/(50 - 40.44) = 0.209$: sell down to about 1,046 shares. A short call has negative gamma, so you buy after rises and sell after falls.

**(d)** Quote above the £4.37 fair value, for example £4.30 bid and £4.45 ask; the client pays the ask. The margin pays for hedging costs and for adverse selection, if the client knows something. It also pays for holding the risk. After the delta hedge, four risks remain. Gamma: large moves between rehedges cost money. Vega: a rise in implied volatility marks the short calls up. Jumps: a gap moves the share before you can trade. Model risk: a coarse tree and a constant $\sigma$ may misprice the call. Parity gives the matching put at $4.37 - 50 + 47.52 = 1.89$, a check on any put you quote.

rubric.text: Bounds the call by $S_0 - Ke^{-rT} = 2.48$ below and $S_0 = 50$ above, with the replication reason.
Works backwards through both steps to about £4.37, discounting each step by $e^{r\Delta t}$.
Hedges with $\Delta_0 \approx 0.644$: about 3,221 shares bought, mostly with borrowed cash.
Rebalances the hedge: delta goes to 1 after an up step and about 0.21 after a down step.
Quotes above fair value for costs, adverse selection or risk, and names two remaining risks (gamma, vega, jumps, model).

explain.text: The bounds frame the price, the tree prices the copy, and the copy is the hedge. Delta changes at every node, so a seller trades again after each move. The quote adds a margin for what the hedge cannot remove.
